## 10. Wave-25 day-two friction (DX8)

Implementer: Codex / Charlie Cheever, 2026-10-23. Commission: wave-25 fix list
8b #1–#13, building on DX7 and Integration 23/24. This amendment is a reviewed
implementation commission, not author acceptance or a publication claim.
The no-JavaScript migration, atomic activation, job-meter and row-lifetime
custody laws above still apply. Integration 23 owns rollback-view selection and
its trigger; SEC9 owns column-write authority, security gates and adversarial
campaign reach. DX8 changes neither of those lanes' policy.

### Migration interpretation and current-value renames

Backfill arguments and lookups read the assembled pre-patch snapshot, before
any simultaneous rename/backfill writes outputs. Historical argument names
therefore name predecessor fields. A declaration's immutable meaning is its
normalized typed-IR digest. Every changed-meaning refusal, both continuously
carried and after a historical gap, prints old and new full digests. A new name
is a new declaration; pruning does not reset names or immutable definitions.
Prune previews name known down projections whose native/reverse or overlapping
forward-preimages they discard. This warning is privileged operator output;
prune remains explicit and destructive, and unavailable evidence still refuses
subsequent reversal/re-entry. Preview never mutates live history.

For the generated `$rename:down` with identical declared old/new scalar types,
the current renamed cell outranks its non-null retained predecessor cell. This
is an identity spelling change, not a historical computation: v1 must see the
edited v2 quote, not the original quote. Stage it on the existing newer snapshot
and preserve native/reverse evidence in the same transaction. Repeated
rollback/forward cycles retain that current value. Different-type renames still
refuse even when sample values happen to fit. Authored down projections retain
their exact forward-preimage/non-null-native precedence; a generated rename
does not grant another declaration permission to replace protected cells.
Conflicting edits under an older view still require an explicit bridge where
existing receipt custody cannot reconcile them. The change stays isolated in
backfills.rs; it does not alter rollback views or release bridges.

### One child per list element

`extract CHILD from PARENT via REF each: {destination:sourceList}` extends the
existing one-child extraction. Exactly one mapped destination is a required
scalar image/file/video; its historical source is a bounded list with an
identical element type (optionally a nullable whole list). Other mapped fields
retain the existing immutable authoritative scalar-copy law. Empty lists create
zero children. A null whole list remains null after an unchanged empty cycle;
a populated child set becomes a real list. Duplicate asset elements refuse:
one asset cannot acquire two child homes. Unsupported types refuse, never copy
or reupload bytes. Default `extract` keeps its existing whole-cell behavior.

Per-parent element receipts bind current asset IDs to stable child lifetimes
and ordinal positions; new historical elements get deterministic child IDs,
independent destination history refuses. Current child asset edits keep their
child ID. Reverse selection gathers every extant child, including native v2
children with valid captured parent-lifetime evidence, preserving receipt order
and appending native children in ID order. It moves current homes back into the
old list and records the current element-to-child map. Returning forward follows
that map, so old-client reordering preserves child identity and appending a new
asset creates one new child. Removed elements mark their receipt-owned child asset absent (an internal null),
leaving the retained child outside the active population under ordinary narrowing; they do not
silently regain an asset or get deleted. A target list that cannot represent
the full current population follows ordinary narrowing, never truncates it.
Every receipt-owned child and its parent-lifetime evidence is validated before
either forward or reverse processing, including removed elements and intact
dormant nulls. A missing/pruned receipt-owned child or invalid parent lifetime refuses rather
than recreating history or recapturing a reused parent ID. Reverse selection
refuses atomically if a populated child asset home remains in narrowed storage;
it names the retained population and requires a loosened child-domain bridge
that restores those rows before selecting old source. Migration-owned null
removals have no live child asset home and stay dormant across repeated cycles.

A successfully applied element extraction records durable definition custody,
including an empty initial population. Temporarily retiring its child table or
declaration suspends that law when the selected parent no longer declares the
source list. Re-entry with the same definition resumes current child rows and
homes rather than demanding or replaying the consumed list. It validates every
receipt and every restored/current child's existing parent lifetime, captured
authority, immutable scalar copies, ledger home and bytes; it never retroactively
captures independent children born while the declaration was absent. Missing
source plus unknown definition refuses. New parents created while the child
table is retired can have zero children. Ordinary narrowed storage remains
retained; no row or home is synthesized. Resuming, as every activation, is atomic
and metered with the child page and parent image sharing its job allowance.

Source/destination read authority and column gates retain the existing strict
extraction checks in both directions, including captured parent-authority agreement. One extraction owns each child table, avoiding competing sources for native children. No user migration endpoint or broader
asset audience is introduced. Per-parent traversal/allocation/writes use job
meters; a cut aborts the entire activation. Home transfers, row changes,
receipts, ordinary reference/narrowing/uniqueness/cap validation and generation
publication share the existing writer transaction. Successful adoption fences
this law with release-store format 10, including after selecting old source;
formats 8/9 remain readable and failed adoption does not upgrade their marker.
No successful later adoption downgrades the marker. Serialized schemas carrying
`each` also require `release-child-extraction-each-v1`, so older engines refuse
the new interpretation before accepting a compiled schema.

### Operator processes, development clock and real accounts

`snapback4 stop <deployment-dir>` uses the existing same-owner authenticated
local release-control channel, then awaits the kernel lock-release barrier.
Already stopped is success. An unverifiable/live foreign owner refuses: never
unlink a lock or signal a guessed PID. Proof hosts/frontends/tool commands own
an explicit process group, including npm wrappers and children. Stop, failure
and parent exit release that entire owned group through live keeper/pipe
custody; cleanup is bounded and cannot silently leave a serving descendant.
Processes deliberately leaving custody are outside that promise. Scripts whose
stdout is one JSON line use `npm run --silent`; logs remain separate.
Changelog/help qualification treats `run` immediately following npm/bun/pnpm
as that package manager’s subcommand; later explicit Snapback invocations
on the same line still advertise flags and remain checked.

A password-authenticated development host exposes clock status/advance with
fixture/persona doors closed. It requires an exact full `service:operator`
bearer token minted through the existing local store authority. Ordinary users,
other seats, read-scoped sessions, unauthenticated requests and production
hosts cannot use it. Staging keeps its existing full-service-seat authorization;
explicit unsafe development and guest-schema development retain their existing local fixture behavior.
Authenticated development jumps preserve live full/read session families and
worker leases by default in the same store transaction as the jump's durable
authority effects; expired/revoked families never revive. Explicit
`sessions: 'expire'` requests expiry testing. Header/SDK reconciliation keeps
current clients alive across the jump. The development offset is process-local
and returns to wall time on restart; staging retains DX7's persistent checkpoint
and paused-drain behavior. A failed/ambiguous jump is never automatically
replayed. `startDev` exposes operator-backed now/advance/drain without opening
fixture doors. Production uses wall time and refuses clock control.

`provisionAccounts` shares seedAccounts plan validation, generated credentials,
identity retry/deadline behavior, result shape, selected seat and provision
mutation. It accepts production through real signup/login and
ordinary authorized mutations; it refuses development and uses no seed/system
bypass; staging continues to use seedAccounts. Custom per-user args retain seedAccounts' existing merge precedence.
A minted service seat is only that exact principal, not a superuser. The served schema exposes `service_identities`, a list of explicit positive
viewer/service equality facts and declared route/schedule seats, excluding result
and enum literals. Both local CLI minting (live or stopped) and the production
helper warn on stderr when a seat has no matching explicit authorization identity.
This is conservative diagnostic evidence, never a proof of admission or denial;
public rules and dynamic application roles still decide actual authority. The mutation's actual read and write rules decide.

### Inspection and saved artifacts

Default active sql/data/releases announce the retained dormant row count when
nonzero. Missing active-table errors identify a retained table and its row count
and name a concrete dormant inspection command. Inspection remains a privileged
read-only consistent snapshot, outside application rules. Only direct,
schema-proven media cells in `sql --json-objects` decode to their ordinary wire
JSON values; positional `--json` remains compatible. Truncation and dormancy
notices go to stderr, preserving JSON stdout; existing limit/more fields stay.

An identical-source deploy with --save-version can refresh an existing saved
version only if the complete Quarry source set and exact bytes match. Differing
source refuses. Generated client artifacts are emitted from that saved source's
Bound, independently of the working tree; fixtures/source evidence stay intact.
Refresh follows successful adoption/no-op and records the correct retained
release identity. Replaying an old source never silently emits the current API.

### Paging, proof assertions and contract advice

Board/roster starters and list recipes use newest-first `last N by .id`, while
explicit oldest-first examples remain labelled. The language's ordering default
does not change. Cursors are opaque evaluator-issued positions: send next back
unchanged; a row id/projection is not a cursor. `exhaustPages(readPage)` begins
with null, gathers array pages, follows next, and refuses denial/loading,
malformed/repeated cursors or its explicit page bound. It never turns a capped
or partial read into complete evidence. Projections change fields, not cursor
meaning/order/completeness.

Day-two recipes compare by stable id across stages and declared common fields,
not list position or whole differently-shaped row images. IDs created by a
frozen v1-client replay are recorded and excluded from preservation baselines.
V2-native IDs may be absent from an exact v1 view; they must reappear unchanged
on forward. Domain-specific synthesized old values need an authored projection
assertion, not an equality claim for incompatible representations.

renderedText(..., null) equals omitted options. Whitespace normalization,
case-sensitive exact matching by default, explicit substring matching and DX7's
legal scroll reachability remain unchanged. The lane-031 full-line regression
must match mounted reachable `Pump logged.` text, without widening hidden clips.
Write-authority hints explain that a mutation require and the caller's table
rule are separate gates. The captured-vs-live-parent card describes existing
lifetime/audience semantics; it grants no new authority.

Old-client INPUT BREAK advice follows accepted wire identities, including
references through declared table renames and lowered aliases/defaults. Real
removed/required/narrowed inputs still warn. Pure object-result field additions
are RESULT NOTE, not RESULT REVIEW or an adoption hazard; changed/removed fields
and domains retain review. These remain conservative advice, not a proof of
unchanged business behavior. No runtime input validation is weakened.

# llp-orient

<!-- @ref https://github.com/ccheever/llp/blob/v0.5.2/llp/0008-distributed-agent-skills.rfc.md#the-skills--core-five-plus-flags — skill contract -->
<!-- @ref https://github.com/ccheever/llp/blob/v0.5.2/llp/0000-linked-literate-programming.explainer.md#2-reference-syntax — the grammar this reads -->

Load the design rationale governing the area you're about to touch, before touching it. This is the consumption side of LLP — orienting first is what turns `@ref` from a possibility into a habit.

Invoke as `/llp-orient <path-or-task>` (file, directory, subsystem, or task description). With no argument, use the current change scope (`git diff --name-only`).

## Trigger

Start of a coding task that touches an area with documented design. The orient-first *rule* lives in the repo's always-loaded `AGENTS.md`; this skill is the detailed form that rule routes to for non-trivial work — don't rely on ambient description-match alone.

## Invariants

- MUST be read-only: never edit code or LLP documents.
- MUST scope to the task: pull the constraints that bind this change, not a corpus summary.
- MUST cite, not restate: reference policy as `LLP NNNN#anchor` rather than paraphrasing sections.
- MUST NOT invent constraints. If something isn't documented, say so.
- MUST NOT guess the rationale behind a broken `@ref` — report it and hand off to `llp-maintain`.

## Workflow

> **Recipe (advisory)** — corpus root = nearest `llp/` walking up from the path in scope (LLP 0001 §Unit of adoption); "no corpus" is an empty walk, not cwd-relative absence. Read `llp/foundation/` first (the kernel; the root LLP is there once `Active` — on a fresh adoption it is still `Draft` and sits in `current/`), then skim `llp/current/` (the declared working set); both hold relative links — symlinks, or small files containing the relative path — so `ls` answers and either form resolves. Then the root LLP's systems vocabulary. `Grep '@ref'` over the files in scope and `Read` each target — these are the highest-signal context. `Grep` the `**Systems:**` headers across `llp/` for LLPs governing the subsystems touched; read the governing ones (Spec, Decision, Principles, relevant RFCs). Follow `Related:` and nearby `@ref` targets one hop out; stop there unless something is clearly load-bearing. Stale-pin nudge (skip offline): read the installed tag from the skills receipt (or a `source:` pin), compare `git ls-remote --tags <origin>` — if upstream is newer, say so in one line ("skills at v0.3.0, upstream v0.5.2 — run /llp-adopt update") and move on; never update from here.

## Artifact

A context pack with these sections, faster to read than the documents it points at:

- **Scope** — files / subsystems queried
- **Governing LLPs** — numbered list, one-line gloss each; mark which are in `foundation/` and which are in `current/` (in-flight — its guidance may still move)
- **Active constraints** — bullets, each citing `LLP NNNN#anchor`
- **Relevant rationale** — the *why*, same citation form
- **Open questions / risks** for this area
- **Likely doc updates** if the change lands
- **Hand-off** — one of `none | llp-adopt | llp-create | llp-review | llp-maintain`

## Hand-offs

- No corpus (no `llp/` walking up from the path in scope) → `llp-adopt`.
- The task needs a decision no LLP covers → `llp-create` (or `llp-review` if proposal-shaped).
- An `@ref` target or anchor doesn't resolve → `llp-maintain`.

# Snapback 4 — agent command sheet

Read this, then [LLP 3000](../llp/3000-snapback4.explainer.md) (the root and
the bakeoff protocol), [LLP 2000.000](../llp/2000.000-keep-the-core-flip-two-substrates.rfc.md)
(the design brief), [`NOT-DOING.md`](./NOT-DOING.md), and the tail of
[`JOURNAL.md`](./JOURNAL.md). `rules/RULES.md` at the repository root is
adopted here as written; LLPs for Snapback 4 are numbered **3000 and up**
(`llp-create --under 3000` for a child; extend LLP 3000 or LLP 2000.000
before minting a new number).

```
cargo build                          # the binary; no JS engine, no bootstrap; crates.io plus one vendored patch (vendor/tiny_http)
scripts/test.sh                      # everything blocking (60 s budget); reports every failure, never fail-fast
./target/debug/snapback4 --help      # init [--online|--expo] · check [--cost|--residency|--fix|--json] · dev · deploy · rollback · serve · run (an op, or a job as the system) · test · why · guide · data · sql · token (a service's seat) · doctor · device · types · --version
./target/debug/snapback4 guide       # lists cards (`guide aliases` lists aliases); `guide language` for the language card — every card's Quarry is compiled by the suite (crates/snapback4-lang/tests/guide.rs)
cd apps/chat && ../../target/debug/snapback4 check     # compiles snapback/*.q, writes snapback/generated/api.ts
cd apps/chat && ../../target/debug/snapback4 dev       # serves 127.0.0.1:4400; re-adopts the schema on save
cd apps/chat && bun run dev                            # the app on the real client (?as=bob picks a persona)
bun run --cwd packages/snapback4 typecheck   # the contract, the client and the hooks typecheck
cargo test -p snapback4-core --test corpus -- --nocapture   # the conformance corpus, with skip reasons
cargo test -p snapback4-difftest     # fixed seeds, oracle regressions and replay (opt-in, no database by default)
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- compile case.q   # a generated or hand-written source's binder diagnostics ("ok" when none)
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- run --seed 0 --cases 100000 --workers 6 --out /tmp/quarry-difftest
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- replay crates/snapback4-difftest/cases/found/rewrite-identity--why--NOT_FOUND
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- run-devices --seed 0 --cases 100000 --workers 8 --out /tmp/quarry-devices   # server against both device stores; no database
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- replay crates/snapback4-difftest/cases/found/device-sqlite--write-predicted-refused--admitted
(cd lean && lake build) && cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- run-lean --seed 0 --cases 100000 --workers 8 --out /tmp/quarry-lean   # the engine against the Lean model (LLP 3000.035 §5.2); ~900 cases/s on 8 workers
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest -- replay 'crates/snapback4-difftest/cases/found/lean--kind--committed~NOT_FOUND'   # needs the model built, or SNAPBACK4_LEAN_ORACLE=<quarry-oracle>
./target/debug/snapback4 check --emit-lean schema.q   # one checked file as the Lean model's case JSON; programs outside its fragment listed with a reason
# Store tests require SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES pointing to a private evaluation cluster.
cargo test -p snapback4-difftest --features postgres  # fails if the cluster is absent
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest --features postgres -- run-stores --seed 0 --cases 1000000 --workers 8 --seconds 10800 --out /tmp/quarry-stores
cargo run --release -p snapback4-difftest --features postgres -- replay /path/to/found-case
python3 scripts/test-difftest-scheduled.py  # runner/ticket tests; no schedule or push
scripts/difftest-scheduled.sh --checkout "$HOME/quarry-difftest-runner" --state-dir "$HOME/.snapback-quarry-difftest" --hours 3
# Operator only: install daily launchd (Darwin) or user systemd timer (Linux).
scripts/install-difftest-schedule.sh --checkout "$HOME/quarry-difftest-runner"
cargo test -p snapback4-sim          # the chat world under faults: the seven invariants
cargo test -p snapback4-sim --test exhaustive   # every sequence of two writes (two viewers, two groups): disclosure and write authority against a model of the rules
SNAPBACK4_EXHAUSTIVE_DEPTH=3 cargo test -p snapback4-sim --test exhaustive -- --ignored   # three writes: ~7,000 states, minutes
scripts/kani.sh [harness...]         # Kani proofs of the key encoding (crates/snapback4-core/src/key_proofs.rs; minutes, ~12 GB peak); outside test.sh
(cd lean && ./check.sh)              # the Lean model of Quarry's core (LLP 3000.035 §5.2): lake build (~15 s cold, needs elan), no-sorry/axiom audit, 53 examples, the quarry-oracle I/O fixture; outside test.sh; open points in lean/OPEN.md
cargo test -p snapback4-sim --test native   # native jobs: builds native-fixtures/rescore for wasm32-unknown-unknown (cold ~20 s, then cached under target/native-fixture) and runs it
bash scripts/build-wasm.sh           # the device as wasm into packages/snapback4/src/wasm/ (the web tier and the Chromium witness need it); fails when the gzip exceeds metrics/wasm-budget.json — a landing that needs the bytes raises the budget in the same commit, with the reason
node witness/idb.mjs                 # the Chromium witness: the client on the wasm device over IndexedDB (needs Chrome)
WITNESS_UDID=<dedicated-udid> node witness/expo.mjs   # published witness verb/helper; freshly install apps/chat-expo Release first (simctl uninstall a previous build: its store belongs to an earlier backend); port 4400, no Metro
node witness/scale.mjs [G] [N] [M]   # cold sync at scale: G groups × N messages × M members into the wasm device; wall time + JS heap → metrics/witness.jsonl
node scripts/measure-storage.mjs     # what the store weighs on the scale seed (rows, indexes, partition log) → metrics/storage.jsonl
                                     # SNAPBACK4_BIN=target/release/snapback4 measures the release build (throughput numbers)
node scripts/measure-client.mjs      # each client tier's bytes on the pinned toolchain → metrics/client.jsonl
node scripts/attribute-wasm.mjs [--families] [--check-families] [--check-absent] # class bytes and concrete serde families; --check-families refuses non-text readers/non-Vec writers outside the exact dynamic-envelope, counting-writer and Scan map-replay allowlists; content-buffer families name the duplicated types and refuse Deserialize representations using untagged, tag or flatten; --check-absent refuses the core's prefetch, admission or log-event symbols in the web artifact (needs twiggy; slow, outside test.sh)
bash scripts/check-release-guard.sh # the web artifact's configuration plus the debug-only `web-device-check` feature must refuse to build (in test.sh)
bash scripts/measure-wasm.sh         # the device core as wasm (crates/snapback4-device), family-checked, bound and measured → metrics/wasm.jsonl
bash scripts/build-xcframework.sh    # the device as an iOS xcframework for packages/snapback4-expo (staticlib alone, stripped; 13.2 MB with native reads)
node loopbar/run.mjs --n 3           # the loop bar: fresh agents on the published pin build reduced Clique M1–M3 → metrics/loopbar.jsonl
node scripts/publish.mjs --prepare-client # rebuild wasm + clean client, pack once for cross-host qualification
# Linux qualification host: strace >=6.8 on PATH (audits every successful TCP listen).
node scripts/qualify-linux.mjs --client /path/client.tgz --expo /path/expo.tgz --out /path/qualification # Linux suite + Ubuntu/Alpine proof, no publish
# Add --consumer-only for packed frontend/toolchain proofs without test.sh; this writes consumer.json, never a publication receipt.
node scripts/publish.mjs             # Mac: qualify/sign Darwin; optional --linux-receipt + --linux-tarball import; platforms before client
```

Crates: `snapback4-core` (value model, schema with `sync`, IR, key encoding,
SQLite store, rules with hoisting, the meter, the interpreter, the partition
log, at-most-once, the day-two classifier, wire forms), `snapback4-lang`
(Quarry lexer, parser, binder, diagnostics, the TypeScript emitter),
`snapback4` (verbs and the HTTP wire), `snapback4-sim` (the deterministic
world hosting the engine and a replica device), `snapback4-difftest` (seeded
Quarry source generator, rewrite and meter oracles, optional Postgres store
oracles with prefetch on/off, the server-against-device oracle on both device stores, the engine-against-Lean-model oracle, structural shrinking and replay; not published or linked by shipped crates), `snapback4-device` (the
interpreter over a `DeviceStore`: the core's SQLite under the native
module for Expo and Exact2 hosts, memory under wasm on the web; one
dispatcher, one suite on both)). The guide (`snapback4-lang/src/guide.rs`) is
the language card and the keyword cards; packages: `snapback4` (the client
over the device and the CLI shim), `snapback4-darwin-arm64` and `snapback4-linux-x64` (the binaries), `snapback4-expo`
(the Swift module over the device's C ABI).

What exists, by week (LLP 3000 §5):

| Week | Lands |
|---|---|
| 1 | the contract (`packages/snapback4/src/contract.ts`), the mocked chat app against it, the hub fixture wrapper, the five floor measurements in the journal, the simulator skeleton (`crates/snapback4-sim`), the Snapback 2 corpus copied in, 0.0.1 published |
| 2 | server: SQLite transaction and interpreter, rules and uniformity, the meter, the partition log (`sync`), generations, personas, the wire, `check`/`dev`/`run`/`test`/`why`/`guide`, the seven simulator invariants |
| 3 | web client: replica store, outbox with client-minted ids, local interpreter, reactive local queries, the online-only tier, the chat app on the real client |
| 4 | Expo client, day-two scenarios, deploy, the loop bar, the Clique hub run, the comparison record |

Gotchas you cannot derive from the code:

- Own Cargo and Bun workspaces; the repository root excludes them. Run cargo/bun from `snapback4/`. Node 24.x (`engines`): run the suite with the pinned runtime on PATH, not the ambient Homebrew node.
- Web builds require `bun install --frozen-lockfile` first. Binaryen 132.0.0 is
  an exact workspace devDependency; build/measurement invoke its portable
  `node_modules/binaryen/bin/wasm-opt` through Node, never a PATH optimizer.
  Missing/mismatched dependencies and optimizer failures refuse the build.
  See README's web-device build instructions and HV round 4 for host parity.
- The suite schedules client files in one pool: `max(1, min(24,
  floor(os.availableParallelism() / 3)))` slots (3 on 10 CPUs, 24 on 96).
  This counts Linux CPU affinity and leaves room for each file's servers,
  browser renderers and workers. Acquisition and server-e2e share that pool;
  there are no extra shard processes outside it. Real-timer files listed in
  `TIMER_CLIENT_FILES` drain that pool and run individually afterward with
  unchanged timing bounds. The quote-jump browser witness remains pooled.
  The two full-count model
  files retain a separate serial slot. `SNAPBACK4_TEST_SERIAL_CLIENT_FILES=1`
  still forces one client file at a time. The external file watchdog measures
  time since a subtest started or finished: max(900 seconds, largest single
  declared guard + max(60 seconds, 25%)). There is no absolute duration cap.
  Console output does not count as progress. Serial mode uses the same bounds.
  See `scripts/run-client-tests.mjs` and the QF round-2 guard census; update
  named work counts and recheck the census when declarations change. Every
  file runs as native `node --test` with default isolation, in a process group
  whose first member is a tiny Node keeper. The runner closes the keeper's stdin
  on completion, stall or abort; only the keeper calls `kill(0, SIGKILL)`.
  Runner death also closes that pipe. An unexpectedly exited keeper fails the
  file and never authorizes a runner signal. Cleanup requires two consecutive
  completed inspections (50 ms apart) with no living group member. Observed leftovers
  fail as TEST_FILE_LEAK. Failed listings and unclassifiable PID/PPID/PGID
  prefixes remain fail-closed. A ps timeout at two seconds retries once with a
  60-second bound; all other command errors refuse immediately. Listings use
  asynchronous spawn so other files' timers and keeper EOF delivery keep running.
  File watchdogs and cleanup's five-second window use per-file monotonic time.
  Expiry requires another completed snapshot: a live group after the deadline
  refuses; two consecutive empty snapshots pass even when the second is late.
  Precisely
  recognized exit-time routing anomalies
  discard the whole snapshot and retry at most twice, 50 ms apart; persistent
  anomalies refuse and never confer ownership (LLP 3000 §7, QF2).
  Metadata is validated for group members and
  their visible descendants; unrelated rows only increment diagnostics.
  Signed Darwin UIDs, variable lstart spacing and comm spaces are accepted.
  Vanished members count as exited. Processes leaving the group (setsid,
  setpgid or detached spawns) are outside cleanup custody; visible descendants
  receive metadata validation but are never signalled by the runner. Native Node's exit
  status alone decides test success; reporter counts are diagnostic only.
  The reporter observes progress as Node delivers it: synchronous work that
  does not yield may buffer events in Node's child until that work finishes.
  Such an unreported interval is subject to the same stall bound. See QF Round 7.
  The M5 MacBook is the publication host; the office M1 is calibration-only.
- Client tests and their helpers must gate Linux APIs (`/proc`, `strace`, `ss`,
  `taskset`, namespace/network tools) at the test or call, or implement a
  portable fallback. Keep portable assertions running on Darwin and give each
  skipped witness an explicit reason. The client pool runs
  `test-platform-audit.test.mjs`: a cheap static census follows static named/namespace `.mjs`
  imports and named helpers and checks scoped Linux skips/branches/early returns.
  A gate in another test does not count. This conservative common-case guard
  does not prove dynamic imports, generated scripts or arbitrary control flow;
  review those paths and run affected tests on the publication Mac.
  Listener snapshots and syscall tracing are Linux qualification capabilities,
  never dependencies of the published `snapback4/proof` browser helper.
- Before a publication dry run, warm the test artifacts **in that publication
  worktree**, while the host is free of calibration work:
  `LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS=-USQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT cargo test --workspace --no-run`.
  Use the dry run's toolchain, target directory, profile/features, `RUSTFLAGS`
  and Cargo profile environment. Do not add `--release` or `--profile production`:
  the suite uses the default test profile. The suite still asks Cargo for the
  complete test inventory, runs every binary and runs doctests separately.
  Warming compiles without executing tests and supplies no qualification receipt.
- One owner on the core (LLP 3000 decision 4): the engine, the store and the client contract are written by the lead session; Codex lanes take the fixture generator, the reference apps, the device witnesses and the periphery. Do not reshape `contract.ts` from a lane; propose the change in the journal.
- No ceiling is raised in slice one (LLP 2000.000 §12). A thing that does not fit changes the design or waits.
- The journal is append-only and dated; never rewrite an entry. LLP 3000 §7 carries decisions that must outlive it.
- Nothing here depends on `snapback2/` at runtime. Copy source deliberately, split under 1,500 lines on the way in, and say so in the journal.
- Named lane: `~/projects/snapback-sb4` on `sb4/*` branches. Never `git stash`; commit checkpoints.
- The conformance corpus (`corpus/`) is Snapback 2's serialized IR and value
  model; the core keeps those serializations so it binds. A case the slice
  cannot run is skipped with a named reason, never counted as a pass.
- `snapback/generated/api.ts` is built by `check` and `dev`, never committed;
  the app's typecheck needs a `check` first (the suite does one).
- Point rule probes and `exists` require a unique key. A fully pinned superset
  of a required unique key is unique too (for example an explicit role index
  containing the unique conversation/principal pair). Nullable unique key
  arguments need non-null proof. Other existence checks use bounded populations
  in code. Named equalities covering a total unique key check extra columns on
  that one row without an additional index.
- The packaged CLI uses `LIBSQLITE3_FLAGS=-USQLITE_ENABLE_MEMORY_MANAGEMENT` during both publication tests and its production build (LLP 3000 §7). A plain production Cargo build retains the dependency's ordinary SQLite policy; use the same build input when comparing with the package. The variable is unnecessary at runtime.
- When creating a stage, `scripts/publish.mjs` runs the suite and refuses on red, builds the production binary, packs `snapback4-darwin-arm64` and verifies the installed digest, then publishes both packages. Bump `version` in `packages/snapback4/package.json` (and its `optionalDependencies`), `packages/snapback4-darwin-arm64/package.json`,
  `packages/snapback4-linux-x64/package.json` and `Cargo.toml` together; a test refuses a mismatch.
- Publication retains exact qualified tarballs under `target/publication/`. If a
  stage exists, use `node scripts/publish.mjs --resume` to validate its recorded
  suite qualification, requalify those exact bytes through the installed-consumer
  proof, and finish missing registry artifacts; an existing version must match
  its staged integrity. This also applies after `--dry-run`. An ordinary invocation
  refuses an existing stage so changed source cannot silently publish old bytes.
  Bump the version to build a new pair; preserve a partially published stage.
- Cross-host publication (LLP 3000.021 §3.3): prepare the common client once
  from clean release source, qualify that tarball on Linux, and import the
  Linux tarball plus its receipt on the Mac. Source commit, client SRI and
  Linux SRI must agree. Linux prefers working Docker/Podman, otherwise uses checksum-pinned proot
  with clean Ubuntu 24.04/Alpine root filesystems in a user cache, and refuses
  `NPM_TOKEN` or `NODE_AUTH_TOKEN`, even when empty. It never signs or packs
  the client. The Mac never rebuilds or executes Linux; `--resume` rechecks
  its copied receipt. No receipt packs a Darwin-only client; an existing
  two-platform preparation is refused on that path. Packed dependencies must
  match the staged set. Uploads use verified private snapshots, with each
  digest checked again immediately before publish.
  Commands and current qualification limits:
  [`reports/20260927-lx-linux-package/REPORT.md`](./reports/20260927-lx-linux-package/REPORT.md).
- The guide is tested text. Every ```quarry block in `crates/snapback4-lang/src/guide.rs` and in `packages/snapback4/README.md` is compiled by `crates/snapback4-lang/tests/guide.rs` with no diagnostic and no note (the language card is also run against the engine); every refusal code the sources emit must be in `guide::CODES`; every `guide("..")` a diagnostic carries must name a card. Add a form to the language card when you add it to the parser, fence README Quarry as ```quarry, and never fence Quarry as plain text to dodge the test.
- Native jobs (LLP 3000.005) need `rustup target add wasm32-unknown-unknown`; the suite's fixture build fails loudly without it. The guest SDK `crates/snapback4-native` is a path dependency until it is published; an app's `snapback/native/Cargo.toml` names it by path.

Quarry store testing (LLP 3000.035 §5.1): `SNAPBACK4_EVAL_POSTGRES` is an
explicit evaluation connection. The factory owns one physical schema per worker,
restores its rows and bookkeeping, installs the compiled fixture, then opens the
ordinary engine. Mutation attempts restore a seeded snapshot; shrinking reuses
that same factory. `Database::connect_fresh()` is an opt-in test mode. Fresh and
restored outcomes must serialize to identical bytes. The local wire observer
retains SQLSTATE, message, detail and SQL statement before the public query API
converts a driver error to a refusal; it never changes the traffic.

Reads sweep every public boundary. Mutations compare every discovered position
twice on SQLite, and compare up to eight seeded positions per dimension on
Postgres (including first/last), plus the case's original budget. Sampling
counters are in `store_stats`; each selected position runs prefetch on and off.
Physical prefetch counters are separate from the exact public outcome record.
The widened generator (`src/widen.rs`) emits prefetch-reachable reads: pages
projecting `tags[.tag]` and `tags[name = .label]` (a `Get` and a unique
`Lookup` whose keys vary across rows) and a loop reading `tags[row.tag]`, so
`store_stats` reports marked reads, transferred rows, cases with a transfer
and `prefetch_consumption_witness_probes` (fewer database calls with prefetch
on: cached answers were consumed). A planted cached-hit-to-miss fault is caught
by the random corpus (LLP 3000.035 §5.1; the closed
[coverage ticket](../issues/closed/20261007-quarry-store-oracle-prefetch-coverage-gap.md)).
Heap is charged identically on every store and the device (LLP 3000.007
§20.24.5); any disagreement is a ticket candidate, never normalized into a pass.
The cluster regression asserts it finds no signature and refuses any new one.

`run-stores --seconds N` stops each worker between cases after N seconds; a case
and any shrinking already underway finish. `cases` remains the requested count,
`generated` is actual completed generation, and `time_limited_workers` reports
the early stop. Slowest-case timing includes generation, comparisons, shrinking
and artifact saving. It does not silently claim the requested million. The scheduled
runner rejects incomplete reports; its own `--hours` option instead chooses a
case count from a 256-case calibration of both campaigns, with 20% headroom and
a million-case cap. This is a sizing estimate, not a hard deadline.

Generator widening (`src/widen.rs`, LLP 3000.035 §5.1): from a stream
independent of the base generator (`generate::base`; a seed it leaves alone is
the base case byte for byte), cases gain prefetch-reachable reads, mutation
blocks (lets, `require`, `if`, several writes to `key` and `k2`, reads after
writes), a prelude of mutations `prep0..` run in order on the same store before
`run` (`Case::steps`, sometimes as the other viewer; `observe` then reads both
keys), and expiry (`expire at .until`, a clock advancing from `seeded_at`
through each step to `clock`, sweeps, `until: now + ttl`). Every oracle runs the
prelude (`execute::world`) and compares its outcomes (`prelude-*` fields;
`store-postgres-prelude`); a device acquires at the seed clock and catches up by
one sync round after the server's prelude. The prelude is emitted first so no
rewrite moves its sites. `lean::generate` narrows half the cases outside the
model (projections, expiry) back into its fragment; the rest stay named
unsupported (`shape`, `loop`, `table-expiry`). The report's `coverage` counts
each new feature (`block/*`, `prelude/*`, `projection/*`, `expire/*`, `clock/*`).

Quarry device testing (`src/devices.rs`, `src/device_writes.rs`, LLP 3000.035
§5.1 oracle 4): each case runs on a server engine and on a device of each store
(native SQLite at a file path, and memory), both brought up through the client's
own path: the `/schema` backend as JSON text, then `local.ts::syncRound` (capture
`sync_state`, `/sync` snapshot pages built as `serve_sync.rs` builds them,
`observe_store`, `apply` through `call_text`, catch-up stream). Never seed a
device store directly. Reads the device publishes without the server (`complete`
with `unknown` false, or a known refusal) compare the whole outcome record
except `seq` (and server-only `delivery`); every other read counts under a named
reason (`online-only-*`). Low ceilings reach the device only through `call`'s
`spent` ledger (`default - n`), compared at the server's boundary positions.
Writes go through `admit`: a device refusal must equal the server's, a
predicted row must equal the committed one (less its `pending` marker), and
after `settle` plus a sync round the device must answer `observe` as the server
does. `run-devices` accepts `--seconds`. Known findings are retained under
`cases/found/device-*` with a `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/devices.rs` replays them
and `tests/smoke.rs` pins the fixed-seed signature set.

The Lean oracle (`run-lean`, LLP 3000.035 §5.2): `snapback4_lang::emit::lean`
translates each generated program's surface tree (never the binder's IR) to
the model's case JSON; `quarry-oracle` (`lean/Oracle.lean`, one process per
worker) answers one tagged outcome per line; the engine runs on SQLite at
default ceilings. Compared: kind, refusal code, data (tagged: an id is not a
text), `complete`, `next` presence, each side's own continuation, and a
mutation's `observe` reread. Not compared: meter fields and sites. Programs
outside the model's fragment are named unsupported reasons, never passes.
`lean::generate` adds Lean-only variants (per-effect rules, a hidden probe
target, nullable/id orders, residual filters) aimed at `lean/OPEN.md`. A
disagreement is a Rust defect, a model defect (only when a document
contradicts the model: fix the model, rerun `lean/check.sh`), or an open
point (record the engine's behaviour in `OPEN.md`); never change the model to
match the engine without a document. Findings live in
`cases/found/lean--*` with `DIAGNOSIS.md`; `tests/lean.rs` replays them and
pins the open signature set. Lean-dependent tests skip loudly without the
built model; `SNAPBACK4_REQUIRE_LEAN=1` makes that a failure.

Quarry scheduled testing: prepare a separate clean clone whose current branch
can fast-forward to `origin/main`. The runner fetches/fast-forwards it and starts
its own socket-only evaluation cluster with `fsync=off`,
`synchronous_commit=off`, `full_page_writes=off`, `shared_buffers=1GB`, and
`max_connections=200`. It builds the Lean model's `quarry-oracle` first
(`lake build` in `lean/`; a host without `lake` fails the run), then runs the
SQLite, store, device and Lean campaigns on the selected
seed window, replays shrunk findings twice, and files/appends open `issues/*.md`
tickets. Only ticket changes are committed/pushed, with three fetch/rebase
retries. State and reports live outside Git under `--state-dir`; seeds advance
only after completed work and successful owned-cluster cleanup. Dirty/diverged
trees, overlap, setup failures, partial reports and failed publication refuse.
A crash can retain the lock and cluster directory; inspect `lock/owner.json`
and the run report. Never stop a cluster by process name.

`--dry-run --cases 32` writes previews and a separate `next-seed.dry-run.json`,
never commits or pushes. Dry runs may explicitly supply `--external-postgres
'host=... user=... dbname=...'`; that cluster is neither started nor stopped by
the runner. Ambient connections do not override normal private-cluster ownership.
The installer remains an operator action; do not invoke it during development.

The Lean oracle on a scheduled host (one-time, per user, no sudo): install
elan with `curl https://raw.githubusercontent.com/leanprover/elan/master/elan-init.sh -sSf | sh -s -- -y --default-toolchain none`.
The runner finds `lake` on `PATH` or in `~/.elan/bin`; the first `lake build`
downloads the toolchain pinned in `lean/lean-toolchain` (Lean 4.34.1, no
Mathlib), so the first scheduled run needs network. Check by hand with

FILE llp/3000.000.000-retained-storage-and-hot-release.rfc.md
876: ## 19. Dormant visibility and migration (DORM)
877: 
878: Implementer: Codex for Charlie Cheever, 2026-10-19; target 0.4.35. This is a
879: proposal until its implementation and two independent READY reviews are
880: recorded. It amends §9.1's prohibition on value substitution only for an
881: explicit, previewed, reversible projection. No inferred coercion is added.
882: The wave-19 day-two evidence distinguishes 21 affected old-client records
883: from retained facts in ten newer-only tables; no row deletion was found.
884: 
885: ### 19.1 Declared old views and renames
886: 
887: Wave-21 EVOL extends this initial surface in [LLP 3000.000.000.002 §8](./3000.000.000.002-declarative-backfills.rfc.md#8-wave-21-release-evolution): active-input refresh, truthful causes, loosened-target bridges, table/asset identity renames and bounded file-text inputs supersede the corresponding initial restrictions below. SEC6 owns security-review resurfacing.
888: 
889: A reverse projection belongs to the newer source and runs when that
890: declaration is left. It reads the assembled newer source under activation's
891: system authority and ordinary job meters, before projection or narrowed
892: visibility closure can hide its inputs. Typed inputs and deterministic point
893: reads follow LLP 3000.000.000.002; simultaneous projections read one snapshot
894: and cannot consume each other's new results. A reverse-only declaration is
895: first-class: moving a legacy field to a related table must not require a
896: dummy forward transformation. Output fields are validated against the
897: selected target schema. Identity, reference lifetime, captured authority,
898: asset and engine-owned fields retain their existing safety boundaries.
899: 
900: The spelling is `down extensions legacyReason(id: id):` followed by
901: `{reason: (explanations[extension = id] ! else MISSING_REASON).explanation}`.
902: Typed inputs describe the current newer row; outputs describe the selected
903: older view, so an old output field need not remain in the newer table.
904: `explanations.extension` must have a unique point index. A declaration is
905: self-contained and immutable by table/name across retained history.
906: Point-read syntax is inherited from LLP 3000.000.000.002 §2: a bare unique
907: `explanations[extension = id]` returns a nullable row, not a scalar field
908: or a silent field fallback. Field access requires the normal non-null
909: proof or `! else CODE`. An explicitly nullable scalar projection can use
910: `{reason: (explanations[extension = id] ! else MISSING_REASON).explanation
911: if exists explanations where .extension = id else null}`. The existence
912: probe is metered on the same source snapshot; its cut refuses instead of
913: selecting the null branch. No new nullable lookup syntax is introduced.
914: This version has no per-release selector for a down declaration: applicability
915: is solely whether the selected same table has the output field. Two writers
916: for that table/field therefore co-apply whenever either can apply; different
917: intended release numbers do not disambiguate them. Reverse output sets on
918: a table are disjoint, including implicit rename writers. Reject overlapping declarations before any adoption work, naming
919: the declarations and field; types do not establish target applicability.
920: Each surviving target cell has at most one reverse writer after saved
921: forward-preimage/non-null-retained precedence. A declaration applies only when the selected target
922: contains its named output; absent target outputs remain retained, not
923: physically introduced into that release.
924: Both raw-schema admission and every activation recheck this condition for
925: the actual candidate/target pair. Computed down outputs are scalar old-view
926: cells only: no reference, asset, collection, identity, captured/maintained,
927: engine-owned or source lifetime output is admitted. A column rename may
928: only move existing lifetime evidence unchanged; it cannot create a binding.
929: 
930: The saved native preimage has the same scalar restriction as the old-view
931: output. A scalar substitution must not archive a newer reference, asset,
932: collection or lifetime-owned cell without custody. A separate scalar column
933: or typed bridge is the repair. Typed reference inputs keep private parent
934: lifetime bindings even when their argument is annotated `id` or an older
935: schema exposes an ordinary id; deleting/reusing that parent cannot authorize
936: recapture on forward or on the next rollback with unchanged inputs. Raw schema
937: validation applies down admission, including unique names, disjoint outputs
938: and sequence ordinals as engine-owned cells. Existence fragments require a
939: declared plain index and a valid prefix/range shape at raw admission;
940: malformed source lookups refuse rather than panic. Every evaluated point/existence lookup sees indexes
941: rebuilt for the assembled source snapshot, including restored rows when no
942: expiry is due. A declaration with no applicable projected cells does not
943: rebuild or validate indexes solely for an expression that will not run.
944: 
945: Rows with saved forward-backfill predecessor preimages use those exact
946: preimages. An entering inactive down receipt likewise restores its exact native
947: cells ahead of another leaving declaration's substitution. Non-null native
948: legacy cells also win over a standalone `down`.
949: A retained value synthesized by an earlier `down` remains owned by its
950: receipt, not a native predecessor preimage. On each later rollback it must
951: be recomputed from current declared newer inputs (including changed point
952: dependencies), with a fresh P receipt. A prior synthesized image never
953: suppresses that recomputation or becomes current truth by precedence.
954: The old synthesized image must still match its receipt before replacement;
955: a conflicting edit aborts rather than silently keeping a stale image.
956: A row whose native restoration never completed still owns its inactive
957: receipt: leaving another narrowed view preserves that receipt and projected
958: image rather than recording its projection as a fresh native preimage.
959: A standalone `down` explicitly authorizes replacing missing/null old-view
960: cells, including an intentionally authored null. This is a declared old-view
961: policy rather than an inference that null is missing: an operator who needs
962: an intentionally null old view must author a nullable expression preserving
963: it. Every physical pre-projection value, including null, is retained as the
964: exact newer-cell preimage in P; physical absence has a distinct marker.
965: Forward restores that original null/absence exactly, so synthesis does not
966: discard its authoritative preimage. No provenance claim distinguishes
967: intentional null from historical manufactured null. Thus nulls
968: materialized and retained by earlier old-source rollback do not suppress it.
969: This is declared synthesis, not a claim about a legacy row's birth release.
970: An asserted lookup for an intentionally null old cell can therefore refuse;
971: authors use an explicitly nullable expression when null is the truthful
972: old view and newer source data is absent. Rows born
973: with the newer representation may use the declared reverse projection.
974: Retain the exact newer projected cells and their reverse result in the same
975: transaction. Compatible forward restores those cells rather than deriving
976: an approximation of their authored value. Unrelated edits under the older
977: source survive. A changed projected cell or a changed dependency that would
978: make its restoration ambiguous refuses atomically with a bridge repair.
979: Deletion/expiry ends the lifetime and clears the corresponding evidence;
980: id reuse never inherits it. Prune previews these private images and leaves
981: reversal-unavailable identities when values are explicitly discarded.
982: Missing lookups, meter cuts and invalid reference/authority evidence refuse,
983: never become false absence. A value with no truthful old representation
984: retains ordinary narrowed dormancy; zero observations do not silently become
985: one observation. The declaration is not a claim that different product
986: meanings are equivalent. All indexes, constraints, read-through validation,
987: maintained data, generation and release selection commit with the projection.
988: 
989: The outcomes are disjoint. A saved forward predecessor preimage wins. Otherwise an
990: eligible row evaluates the declared expression: an asserted missing point
991: executes its authored refusal and aborts activation; an ordinary nullable
992: point may return null only where the expression explicitly allows it.
993: There is no implicit missing-lookup fallback. A successfully computed value
994: that does not fit the old type follows narrowed dormancy. Invalid/corrupt
995: evidence and authority/lifetime failures abort. A meter cut aborts the entire
996: transaction with the ordinary bounded-work refusal; retrying unchanged
997: inputs is not promised to succeed, and an indexed bridge is the repair.
998: Exact retained native cells win on re-entry; an older-source edit to their
999: declared dependencies that conflicts with that native image refuses rather
1000: than deriving over it. An out-of-domain older dependency edit is still a
1001: conflict; hiding that row under the narrower newer type does not authorize
1002: recapture. Pruned evidence requiring discarded values refuses
1003: explicitly, including in later previews; it never fabricates null/default.
1004: Carrying an active pruned declaration through an unrelated schema change
1005: does not need discarded values while its native cells remain available.
1006: Reintroducing a retired native cell still requires actual retained evidence.
1007: Dependency verification, projection and native eligibility marking also visit
1008: already narrowed row images. Adding a declaration while a native row is
1009: hidden must not skip its later projection. Retired inputs use their retained
1010: source definition, including the default interpretation of physical absence.
1011: Hiding a row or retiring an input column cannot bypass a conflict.
1012: For each row, let P be exactly the applicable fields computed by down after
1013: preimage precedence, including outputs which fail the old target domain
1014: and therefore make the row dormant. Their native preimages and computed
1015: results remain receipt-owned even while the row is narrowed. Re-entry
1016: assembles that retained projected row, verifies the same receipt, restores
1017: its native P cells, then applies destination narrowing/validation. It must
1018: not discard P merely because its old-view value is not visible. Its receipt stores each field's newer value or physical
1019: absence and its old-view result. Forward first verifies every field in P
1020: still has exactly the physical presence and value of that old-view result
1021: (absent, present-null and present-default are distinct; interpretation
1022: through a default cannot make them equal),
1023: then restores only P. Receipt-owned physical absence survives later
1024: narrowing, column retirement and whole-row restoration; an older literal
1025: default must not become its native value. Candidate validation interprets
1026: that absence through the native destination definition while the retained
1027: image keeps it physically absent. Individual dormant cells and whole-row
1028: archives must agree on each receipt-owned patch/inverse before either can
1029: be overlaid into a source snapshot. Fields outside P keep the current
1030: old-source values.
1031: Any conflicting field aborts the entire activation; a disjoint field edit
1032: does not authorize overwriting a conflicting projected field.
1033: 
1034: A column rename is declared, never inferred from similar names or types.
1035: The spelling `newName: Type renamed from oldName` names its old column;
1036: both directions preserve the
1037: authoritative cell and lifetime evidence through the same reversible
1038: adoption. A conflicting already-present target value refuses rather than
1039: choosing a winner. Required fields do not acquire invented defaults. Client
1040: argument compatibility is distinct from result shape compatibility: an old
1041: query's result field cannot be promised merely because stored data moved.
1042: Old operation wrappers/projections and the compatibility report must reflect
1043: the actual exposed result shape. Devices execute no migration metadata;
1044: semantic capability/store fences refuse runtimes that cannot interpret the
1045: new declarations or retained evidence.
1046: 
1047: The rename is strictly within the same table and row lifetime; its grammar
1048: names a column, never another table/row/parent. Cross-parent and cross-table
1049: moves are not renames. Identical cell types means the full structural type
1050: including numeric/text bounds, enum members, nullability and nominal target,
1051: not merely its base kind. Existing default/constraint validation still
1052: applies to the selected schema; the rename never invents a missing cell
1053: from a new default, truncates or coerces it. A type conversion needs
1054: a separately declared transformation; the rename itself never converts.
1055: The paired rename form uses the same closed scalar/lifetime boundary as
1056: computed down: references, assets, collections and engine-owned/maintained
1057: columns reject during compilation, before either direction can activate.
1058: This initial surface never accepts a forward-only protected rename.
1059: A missing required source cell without saved evidence/default is E_ADOPT,
1060: not an invented optional value. Old and new target schemas validate their
1061: respective view in each direction.
1062: 
1063: ### 19.2 Forward and captured read-through authority
1064: 
1065: Selecting a newer retained source after older-source writes re-enters its
1066: declared backfills. Newly written old-source rows receive required outputs;
1067: changed old-source inputs or lookup dependencies catch up under the existing
1068: cohort/preimage conflict rules. Native newer outputs remain authored values.
1069: This is not a continuously running trigger and does not synthesize a missing
1070: application side-table fanout job. A schema that needs such reconciliation
1071: must declare/prove it or retain a compatible bridge; it cannot claim required
1072: labels have been supplied merely because retained rows returned.
1073: 
1074: Changing only a read predicate, including narrowing it then selecting the
1075: older predicate, must not itself make captured read-through rollback refuse.
1076: The reference identity, parent lifetime and authority provenance remain
1077: bound. Reusing another parent, resurrecting an expired capture, or changing
1078: capture structure does not qualify as a predicate-only change. Preserve old
1079: captures; do not recapture a broader grant as a side effect of rollback.
1080: Actual target read rules still authorize every read and the preview warns
1081: when selecting older rules restores broader confidentiality exposure.
1082: The operator is the existing same-UID filesystem owner, already capable of
1083: editing the deployment database directly; activation is not a lesser data
1084: role. This amendment adds no new capability/confirmation for selecting old
1085: rules. Predicate-only means unchanged reference/capture structure and
1086: bound parent lifetime/provenance; only the parent read predicate differs.
1087: Writing the down declaration explicitly authorizes its old-view synthesis;
1088: it is not inferred from a type match. Previews list transformed reverse
1089: cells/rows separately from restoration and display lost confidentiality
1090: clauses. Target rules are the selected source's rules: choosing old source
1091: can intentionally broaden access, as before this amendment. The author's
1092: commission does not introduce a second acknowledgment flag or an audience
1093: containment proof for an explicitly authored operator migration.
1094: 
1095: ### 19.3 Exact visibility before mechanical diffs
1096: 
1097: Rollback preview leads with `N records visible under release C will be
1098: hidden from release T users`. Count only before-active authoritative rows
1099: that become retained dormant in a table T has; show each table and bounded
1100: ids in JSON. Separately count surviving target-visible cells that become
1101: null/default or newly lack a retained legacy cell, and rows in tables T
1102: does not have. The empty-cell category separates newly empty/defaulted cells
1103: from restored empty legacy cells; the latter are not claimed as lost text.
1104: Legacy stores cannot distinguish intentionally null old cells from nulls
1105: materialized by an earlier rollback. Report the exact view without inventing
1106: that provenance. This category counts cells, not distinct records across columns.
1107: Actual expiry/deletion and rebuilt private caches are excluded from dormant
1108: loss. Counts precede read rules and are table populations, never a promise
1109: about a particular viewer's query results. Legacy stores lack reliable
1110: row-birth release provenance, so the preview says `visible under`, not
1111: `created under`. An old column newly shown as null is a factual view change;
1112: the tool does not infer which related business text the application wanted.
1113: Hidden-row counts and surviving-cell counts are disjoint by row presence;
1114: newer-only rows have a table absent from T and cannot also be old-table
1115: losses. No jobs or expiry run on dormant rows (§4). On reactivation the
1116: original source deadline still applies: an expired lifetime can retire then,
1117: and retention never promises that expired records revive indefinitely.
1118: 
1119: Each affected class names reverse projection or an expand/contract bridge
1120: as the repair. Rule/guard/operation diffs follow it. Deploy preflight also
1121: warns before future writes to new tables, widened domains or missing old
1122: fields can make a later rollback hide rows or show empty/defaulted cells.
1123: For these three syntactic risk classes the warning is conservative: no
1124: false negatives for new tables, widened value domains and removed old fields;
1125: a fitting authored projection may make a warning a false positive.
1126: Exact reverse adoption on the post-deploy snapshot reports current effects
1127: separately from conservative future-write risks. Previews use MAIN tables
1128: in their private disk snapshot: read-through's connection-local temp-store
1129: configuration cannot erase their before image. All scratch disappears on
1130: success or refusal. Nothing changes live rows, pointers, history or time.
1131: 
1132: ### 19.4 Operator inspection and retained identity
1133: 
1134: `sql --dormant --release DIR` and `sql --all-releases --release DIR` are
1135: mutually exclusive read-only operator views under one pinned SQLite read
1136: snapshot. The first contains retained whole/narrowed rows and retained cells;
1137: the second includes active and retained images. Removed table names and
1138: retained column names are queryable through generated logical application
1139: relations; internal namespaces remain unavailable to submitted SQL. Factual
1140: state/source metadata distinguish active rows, dormant rows and dormant
1141: cells. A retained-cell record contains its id and retained cells, with
1142: unprovided columns null. Conflicting images are separate labelled records,
1143: never an arbitrary winning value. Inspection-mode reserved-name collisions
1144: refuse instead of shadowing application columns. These modes bypass read
1145: rules as existing owner-only SQL does; they add no HTTP/client namespace.
1146: `all-releases` means every image still retained, not time-travel snapshots
1147: or one invented version of every row per historical release.
1148: `_snapback_columns` is the JSON array of actually provided application cells
1149: on each inspection record, so a retained null is distinguishable from an
1150: unprovided SQL NULL. This is provenance, not a missing-value substitution.
1151: 
1152: Equivalent retained executable source remains selectable across compiler
1153: upgrades. Compiler reports or equivalent old/new packaging metadata do not
1154: change source identity; actual source, native and worker behavior remain
1155: identity-bearing and full control-request integrity still covers all files.
1156: Ordinary refused deploys leave neither numbered candidates nor stages.
1157: This is a source-bundle identity, not a frozen compiler-binary identity or
1158: a proof of behavior equivalence between compiler versions. Activation
1159: recompiles retained source with the selected runtime and revalidates every
1160: data/authority constraint. Actual compiler semantic fixes can change
1161: execution without minting a new source id; version negotiation and the
1162: normal upgrade/publication qualification remain independent fences.
1163: Backfill/reverse definition identity still includes its normalized typed
1164: IR. Recompilation that changes that historical definition cannot reuse its
1165: old receipts: immutable-name checks refuse and require an explicit new-name
1166: bridge. Selecting the source id across an upgrade is supported; success of
1167: an incompatible historical migration after an arbitrary semantic compiler
1168: change is not promised. Removing the source-identity trap does not bypass
1169: these admission checks.
1170: 
1171: ### 19.5 Argument aliases and review evidence
1172: 
1173: `explanation: text 1..500 alias reason` declares one canonical argument and
1174: one accepted old spelling on a Quarry query/mutation. Normalize the old
1175: spelling to the canonical value before typed execution, including local
1176: device execution. Both spellings supplied at once refuse E_INPUT even if
1177: equal. Alias names must be unique and cannot collide with canonical args;
1178: deprecated/aliased combinations refuse. Canonical default/null validation
1179: semantics are unchanged. Generated TypeScript accepts either spelling and
1180: rejects both; capability comparison recognizes the old shape accepted by
1181: the alias. Compatibility advice for renamed same-typed inputs recommends
1182: mapping with an alias. It never recommends accepting and dropping the old
1183: value with `deprecated` as a rename repair.
1184: 
1185: Every changed guide fence/starter runs as written against a freshly packed
1186: tarball. Qualification includes regression stores, actual old callers,
1187: reverse/native/preimage conflicts, forward old-source writes, inspection,
1188: hot/cold/check parity and copied wave-19 dormant lanes. Full test and
1189: differential results and any external qualification limits belong in
1190: WORKSTREAM-REPORT.md. Reviews are mutually blind Muse and fresh Codex
1191: sessions on one immutable semantic revision, retained verbatim with
1192: provenance. A READY verdict records review readiness, not author acceptance
1193: or a publication receipt. No version bump or push is authorized.
